# The Hateful Immortals

### A Documentary Study of the Greenbriar-Chen Marriage, 1847–Present

*Compiled and annotated by Dr. Amelia Thornton, Ph.D.*
*Department of Parahuman Studies, Columbia University*
*Published on the occasion of the couple's 177th wedding anniversary, which neither spouse has agreed to celebrate.*

---

## I.

The earliest surviving image of Margaret Greenbriar and James Chen together is a quarter-plate daguerreotype, silver on copper, taken in the studio of one Josiah Harwick on Tremont Street, Boston, in the autumn of 1849. The couple had been married two years. They stand before a painted backdrop depicting a colonnade that neither of them would have mistaken for architecture they had ever seen, which was, of course, the fashion. James wears a dark frock coat with silk facings, buttoned high against a stock collar that appears, even across the frozen chemistry of 174 years, to be bothering him. Margaret wears a day dress of what she has since identified as "mouse-colored challis, rather good, with pagoda sleeves I later regretted," her dark hair parted severely at the center and gathered at the nape. Her right hand rests on James's left forearm. His left hand covers hers.

The posture is conventional for the period. I note it only because it has become, through the peculiar irony of duration, unconventional: in the most recent verified photograph of the couple together—a surveillance-camera still from a Whole Foods in Portland, Oregon, captured in 2013 and subsequently leaked to the *Oregonian*—they are standing approximately four feet apart in the checkout line, and Margaret appears to be reading the ingredients on a box of crackers with the focus of a woman who has decided that the ingredients on a box of crackers are more interesting than the man beside her.

This is a study of a marriage. It is, more precisely, a study of what marriage becomes when it cannot end—not because the participants are unwilling to end it, though both have at various points claimed exactly this, but because their particular conditions render the conventional exits largely theoretical. Margaret Greenbriar does not age. James Chen cannot die. These are not metaphors. They are parahuman capacities, manifest at puberty, clinically documented, and, in the context of this study, as unremarkable as height or handedness. Roughly 0.07 percent of the global population develops such capacities. The literature on the sociological implications is extensive; I will not rehearse it here.[^1] What concerns us is the specific case: two such individuals, married young, still married, and by most available accounts profoundly tired of each other in a manner that has less in common with ordinary marital fatigue than with the deep weariness of continental plates that have been grinding against one another for geological ages and have not yet produced a satisfactory mountain range.

[^1]: For a comprehensive overview, see Parekh and Yamamoto, *The Powered Population: Epidemiology, Taxonomy, and Social Integration* (Oxford UP, 2019). For the specific taxonomy of longevity-class capacities, see Greenbriar-Chen's own intake file at the Parahuman Registry, Boston Office, dated 1911, which classifies her ability as "eidetic persistence, temporally unbound, with concomitant biological stasis"—a description she has called "clinically accurate and spiritually bankrupt."

The daguerreotype repays close inspection. The exposure would have required fifteen to thirty seconds of absolute stillness, during which the subjects were instructed to fix their gaze on a stationary point and suppress all expression. Most daguerreotype portraits carry the resulting rigidity like a mask; the subjects look embalmed. In the Greenbriar-Chen plate, something has gone slightly wrong. Margaret's mouth is not quite set. The left corner is compressed in a way that is invisible at a glance and unmistakable under magnification: she is suppressing a laugh. Her eyes—directed not at the camera but fractionally to the left, toward James—are bright with the effort of containment.

I asked her about this. I was not the first to ask; the daguerreotype has been reproduced in at least three prior studies, and the anomalous expression has been noted by scholars more eminent than myself, including Dr. Lois Kader, whose 2004 monograph on parahuman longevity and domestic life remains the standard reference.[^2] But I was, apparently, the first to ask with a recording device running, in a formal interview setting, under conditions governed by the Columbia IRB protocol for parahuman subjects, which Margaret Greenbriar tolerates with the patience of a woman who has endured many formal frameworks imposed upon her life and no longer has the energy to find them offensive.

[^2]: Kader, L., *The Unending Household: Domestic Life Among Long-Lived Parahumans* (Chicago UP, 2004), pp. 112–14. Kader's analysis of the daguerreotype focuses on James's posture and concludes, persuasively if somewhat drily, that he "appears to be enjoying himself." One might say the same of most surviving images of James Chen across any century. The man photographs well. Margaret has noted this with what I can only describe as profound irritation.

She said: "The studio smelled like iodine and lavender oil. The lavender was Mr. Harwick's attempt to mask the iodine vapors from the sensitizing process—he fumed the plates himself, in a closet behind the posing room. It didn't work. The iodine cut through it completely. There was also mercury, though you couldn't smell that; I only learned later what it was, and by then Mr. Harwick was dead of it, which was common among daguerreotypists, though nobody had made the connection yet." She paused. She adjusted the position of her teacup on its saucer with the specificity of a woman placing a decimal point. "James leaned toward me just before the exposure. Mr. Harwick had already removed the lens cap. James knew perfectly well we were supposed to be still. He whispered something."

I asked what he had whispered.

"No," she said.

In the published transcript of this interview—which I include in the appendix and which has been verified by both subjects—the word "No" is followed by approximately four seconds of silence, during which the recording captures the sound of the teacup being adjusted again, a breath, and what may be the beginning of a word that is abandoned before it becomes identifiable.

I did not press the question. This proved wise. One learns, in the study of the Greenbriar-Chen marriage, that the materials resist the scholar at precisely the points where they are most essential. Margaret's memory is, by any clinical measure, perfect. She can recall the chemical formula of the sensitizing solution (a saturated iodine vapor applied to the silver-coated plate), the thread count of her challis dress, the number of steps between the street entrance and Mr. Harwick's posing room (fourteen, with a turning at the seventh), and the precise sentence her husband whispered during a fifteen-second exposure 175 years ago. She will provide all of these details freely, at length, with the weary generosity of a woman who has been asked about herself by scholars for the better part of a century and has made a kind of peace with it. But the sentence itself—the one that caused the suppressed laugh, the one that is visible in the silver, the one that has survived the disappearance of the studio, the building, the street, the daguerreotypist, the city as it then existed, and every other person who was alive that day—this she withholds.

I respect the boundary. I also note it. In a marriage of 177 years, the truly private archive is not what has been forgotten. It is what is perfectly remembered and refused to the record.

---

James Chen, interviewed separately at his residence in Asheville, North Carolina—they have maintained separate dwellings since 2019, though Margaret calls this "a sabbatical, not a separation," and James calls it "the best idea either of us has had since Buenos Aires"—had this to say about the daguerreotype:

"Sure. Josiah Harwick. Tremont Street. Maggie looked beautiful. Do I remember what I whispered?" He grinned. This is documented in my field notes because the grin itself seems to constitute a significant portion of the James Chen archival record; interviewers across multiple decades have noted it. It is, by all accounts, an exceptional grin. The visual anthropologist Dr. Rena Okafor-Baptiste has described it as "a grin with its own foreign policy."[^3] "I don't remember," he said. "But it must have been pretty good, because she's still mad about it."

[^3]: Okafor-Baptiste, R., personal correspondence, 2023. She added: "The man is infuriating. His wife is correct to be annoyed."

I asked him to clarify whether "mad" meant angry or something else.

"Doc," he said, "we've been married 177 years. Those words don't mean different things anymore."

---

A note on what follows. This study was undertaken with the cooperation—not the enthusiasm, but the cooperation—of both Margaret Greenbriar and James Chen, who signed release forms, sat for interviews totaling some forty-six hours of recorded material, and granted access to what Margaret calls "the archive" and James calls "the boxes Maggie won't let me throw away." The archive is extensive. It occupies a rented storage unit in Durham, North Carolina, and contains personal correspondence, private journals, legal documents, financial records, newspaper clippings, seventy-one photographs spanning four different photographic technologies, marginalia in 214 books, the lease for a vineyard in Mendoza province, a grocer's receipt from 1903 with a single word written on the back in James's hand (the word is "sorry"), and a human-trafficking dossier compiled by the Pinkerton National Detective Agency in 1882 at the request of Margaret's sister, who believed James had kidnapped her. He had not. They had moved to London. But the sister's concern was not unreasonable; the marriage was two decades old, Margaret still appeared to be twenty-three, and no one had offered Mrs. Eleanor Fairfield of Beacon Hill a satisfactory explanation because no satisfactory explanation was yet possible. The Pinkerton report is sixty-four pages long and concludes, with evident frustration, that "the subject appears to be neither captor nor captive but merely a husband, a condition which this agency is not equipped to further investigate."

I mention the archive's breadth because the study that follows is, necessarily, not broad. A marriage of 177 years resists comprehensive treatment the way a river resists being carried in a bucket. What follows is a selection: five exhibits, drawn from the record, arranged not chronologically but emotionally—by weight, by pressure, by the principles that seem to me, after two years of immersion in the material, to govern the structure of this particular shared life. I present them with the usual scholarly apparatus. I hope the apparatus is sufficient. I suspect, at this point, that it is not.

---

## II.

On the morning of March 14, 1871, Mrs. Ada Colquitt of 34 Chestnut Street, Boston, remarked to Mrs. Patience Hewitt of 36 Chestnut Street that Margaret Greenbriar-Chen, their neighbor these past eleven years, had not aged. Mrs. Colquitt had been thinking about it since the previous Sunday, when she had encountered Margaret at the milliner's and had been struck by what she described, in a letter to her sister in Albany, as "the most unnatural freshness."

The full letter, dated March 16, 1871, reads in relevant part:

> *I do not mean she looks well. Many women look well. I mean she looks precisely as she did when they arrived on the street in 1860 & I do not mean in the general way that one says a person "hasn't changed" — I mean the line at the corner of her left eye that I noticed at our first meeting is still there, the same line, in the same place, to the same depth, and there is no other line beside it or near it. It is the exact same face. I have been turning this over for four days and I am not a fanciful woman Eleanor, you know I am not, but it has unsettled me considerably & I told Patience Hewitt who said I was being foolish but looked quite pale when she said it.*

James and Margaret were gone within twelve days.

The speed of this departure is characteristic. James handled the practical elements with a competence that Margaret has described, in different interviews across a span of decades, as "efficient," "ruthless," "almost hurtful in its ease," and "the thing about James that I have never decided whether to admire or despise." He sold the house to a Mr. Thomas Garrett for a sum that Margaret still considers insultingly low. ("He could have gotten at least eight hundred more. The garden alone was worth—but he didn't care. He never cares about the money from the place we're leaving. He only cares about the money at the place we're going.") He booked second-class passage on the *RMS Scotia*, departing Boston for Liverpool on March 26. He selected London as their destination, based on what he described to Margaret as "the population density and the British constitutional aversion to asking personal questions." He was, by Margaret's account, cheerful. He was, in fact, "whistling."

"Whistling what?" I asked.

"'Shoo Fly, Don't Bother Me.' The full arrangement. All the verses. He invented a third verse that didn't exist, about a fly who traveled to London and found the weather agreeable. He thought this was hilarious."

"Was it?"

"I was packing the contents of our home into six trunks, Dr. Thornton. No, it was not."

---

The packing is documented. Margaret had written, on the morning of the 15th—less than twenty-four hours after Mrs. Colquitt's remark, before James had even finalized the sale—a list of items she wished to take. The list survives in the archive. It is four pages long, written in an ink that has barely faded, in a hand that is recognizably the same hand as the one that signed her interview release form in my office in 2023. It is organized not by category but by room, and within each room not by utility but by what I can only describe as a private emotional taxonomy whose governing principles are not immediately legible to an outside reader. From the kitchen: a tin grater (ordinary), a ceramic bowl with a chip in the rim "from when J dropped it, March 1862" (ordinary), and a cutting board made of maple that had been a gift from a woman named Harriet Baylor, "who brought it when she came to dinner on the night Lincoln was shot and who held my hand afterward and said nothing, which was exactly right, and who died of typhus in 1867, and who I will not leave behind in the form of this cutting board." From the parlor: a cushion she had embroidered herself, a brass candlestick, and "the red book," identified elsewhere in the archive as a copy of *Aurora Leigh* that James had given her the year they married. From the bedroom: "the quilt from J's mother." Nothing else from the bedroom. Either the bedroom contained nothing else of value, or the items of value from the bedroom are among the things Margaret Greenbriar chooses not to give the record.

James's packing list does not survive, because James did not make one. When I asked him what he brought to London in 1871, he said: "Clothes. Money. Margaret. What else would I need?"

"Nothing sentimental? No keepsakes?"

He considered this. "I brought my pocketknife. Swiss-made. Good blade. Lost it somewhere in Bermondsey in—I want to say '74? '75? Doesn't matter. Got another one."

I noted that Margaret's list ran to four pages.

"Sure," he said. "Maggie packs like she's building a museum. I pack like I'm catching a train. We've had this argument. We've had it—" He stopped. He did something I had not previously observed in roughly fourteen hours of interviewing James Chen: he paused. His face did something complicated. Then the grin returned, smaller than usual, and he said: "We've had it a lot."
